unit.name: Probability & Comparing Distributions
unit.subtitle: From the 0–1 scale to two-way tables, tree diagrams, Venn diagrams, risk communication, the Normal distribution and Petersen capture–recapture.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students plot frequency on the y-axis of a histogram with unequal class widths instead of frequency density (frequency ÷ class width). Examiner reports flag this repeatedly as a multi-mark drop.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Statistics 8382 assessment guidance, allaboutmaths.aqa.org.uk (accessed 2026)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students treat stratification as a sampling method. The spec is explicit that stratification is a method used BEFORE sampling takes place. The downstream technique is then random sampling within each stratum.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Statistics 8382 specification, B3f Notes

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students treat strong correlation as proof of causation. Correlation does not necessarily imply causation (spec E8c). Multiple factors may interact.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Statistics 8382 specification, section E8c

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students plot at the start or end of each class rather than at the midpoint. One of the most common errors in Section C data-representation questions.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Statistics 8382 teaching guidance, allaboutmaths.aqa.org.uk (accessed 2026)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students state "X has a higher mean than Y" without interpreting what that means in context. Spec E3 explicitly demands context-based interpretations, not just observations of difference.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Statistics 8382 specification, E3b–E3c Notes

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students use the wrong formula for quartile position with small n. The spec controls this by ensuring exam data sets have n one less than a multiple of 4.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Statistics 8382 specification, D3a Notes

common_misconceptions.topic: Tree diagrams with and without replacement
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students keep denominators unchanged on the second branch when sampling without replacement, leading to systematic errors in conditional probability questions.
Students confuse a "doubled relative risk" with a large absolute increase. Doubling 1 in a million to 2 in a million is small in absolute terms.
common_misconceptions.source: Royal Statistical Society teaching resources on risk communication, rss.org.uk (accessed 2026)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students apply the formula but cannot state the assumptions: closed population, equal probability of capture, no loss of tags. The assumptions question is worth separate marks.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Statistics 8382 specification, E12d Notes

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students assign the same rank to tied values rather than the mean of the ranks they would have occupied, systematically distorting Σd² and the final coefficient.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Statistics 8382 teaching guidance, allaboutmaths.aqa.org.uk (accessed 2026)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students miss that one symbol represents more than one item, then divide instead of multiplying. The single most common Foundation-tier 1-mark drop on Section C questions.
Higher students calculate the standard deviation but cannot interpret what it tells them about spread relative to another set with the same mean.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Statistics 8382 specification, E3b Notes (HT)

student_errors_by_question_type.2 marks — Calculate: Students show full working but forget to clearly state the final answer, or round too early. Method marks are usually awarded but accuracy marks are lost without a clear final value.
student_errors_by_question_type.3 marks — Show That: Students reach the target value but omit the intermediate step. "Show that" demands each step be explicit — answer-only responses score zero.
student_errors_by_question_type.3 marks — Describe: Students describe what is on the graph without describing what it shows about the data. Examiners want trend + context (e.g. "house prices rose steeply between 2010 and 2015", not "the line goes up").
student_errors_by_question_type.4 marks — Compare in Context: Generic comparisons do not score full marks. Students must (1) state the comparison numerically, (2) interpret it in the context of the question. Two comparisons (one of central tendency, one of spread) is the standard expectation.
student_errors_by_question_type.4 marks — Explain: Students give a single point when the question asks for two distinct points each elaborated. The mark scheme typically awards two marks per developed point.
student_errors_by_question_type.5 marks — Suggest and Justify: Students suggest an improvement but justify it with a generic comment ("it would be more accurate"). Examiners need the justification to refer to the specific issue raised — link to bias, sample size, response rate or measurement error.
student_errors_by_question_type.6 marks — Discuss: One-sided answers cap at half marks. Students must present at least two considerations and reach a judgement.
student_errors_by_question_type.8 marks — Statistical Enquiry Cycle Crit: Students describe what the enquiry did rather than evaluate. The structure that scores Mastering: identify a weakness at each of two SEC stages, explain why each weakens the conclusion, suggest a specific improvement.

topic_weighting_notes: Paper 1 and Paper 2 each carry 80 marks (50% of the GCSE) and assess all specification content. Each paper ends with a Statistical Enquiry Cycle question integrating content from multiple sections.

AO1 (knowledge and recall) approximately 55%, AO2 (interpret in context and draw conclusions) approximately 25%, AO3 (assess methodology via the SEC) approximately 20%. More than 45% of marks come from interpretation and methodology, not pure calculation.

Section C (representing data) and Section D (numerical measures) account for the majority of calculation marks. Frequency density, cumulative frequency/IQR/box plots, and tree diagrams are highest-frequency calculation topics on Paper 1.
SEC critique and comparing distributions in context are the highest-frequency interpretation topics on Paper 2.

Higher-only topics with substantial mark weighting: histograms with unequal class widths (frequency density), standard deviation, Spearman’s rank, Normal distribution, capture–recapture, conditional probability notation.
current_spec_changes: Spec 8382 has been in delivery since June 2019 exams (Version 1.1, 26 Feb 2018) and has not undergone a content revision since. Reference resources from 2017–2026 remain authoritative.
Calculator policy: students may use statistical functions but it is not a requirement (section 5.9). Standard deviation can be obtained from calculator stat functions.
pedagogical_notes: EEF guidance recommends explicitly teaching common misconceptions rather than side-stepping them. Every practice deck should contain at least one problem targeting a known misconception with a clear explanation of the wrong answer.
Two or three worked examples per new technique gives a greater learning effect than one alone (EEF "FAME" approach). The Bronze/Silver/Gold worked example structure already aligns with this.

Statistical interpretation is the dominant weakness in school statistics teaching. Practice deck silver and gold problems must privilege context-based interpretation prompts over additional procedural practice.

Dual coding (pairing verbal and graphical representations) is especially powerful for distribution-shape topics. Present skew, Normal distribution and box plots in words, diagram, and summary statistic simultaneously.
Retrieval practice spaced across the two-year course is more effective than blocked end-of-unit revision for statistics calculations, which are highly procedural and decay quickly.
spec_gaps: A1: null-hypothesis notation explicitly excluded by spec — content agents must NOT introduce H_0 notation anywhere in content_html.
C1b: 3D comparative representations are interpretation-only (spec excludes drawing) — do not ask students to draw 3D charts.
E13b: distribution of sample means covered intuitively only; no formal X-bar notation — article lesson covers this at a conceptual level only.

lessons_in_batch.title: Probability Scale, Expected Frequency and Estimating from Data
lessons_in_batch.description: Using the 0–1 (or 0–100%) scale, calculating expected frequency, and estimating probability from observed data.
section_markers: experimental probability tends to theoretical probability

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Foundation core: scale and expected frequency. Experimental probability → theoretical as number of trials increases when all variables are random. Use estimation from a relative frequency table as a hinge problem.

lessons_in_batch.title: Relative Risk, Absolute Risk and Risk Communication
lessons_in_batch.description: Calculating relative and absolute risks, expressing them as expected frequencies in groups, and reading risk in the media.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Real-world health-statistics framing. Worked examples should expose the classic "doubles the risk from 1 in a million to 2 in a million" gotcha to make the absolute/relative distinction concrete.

lessons_in_batch.title: Two-Way Tables, Tree Diagrams and Venn Diagrams
lessons_in_batch.description: Representing up to three events with two-way tables, sample-space diagrams, tree diagrams and Venn diagrams, including conditional probability for Higher.
section_markers: P(A and B) equals P(A) times P(B)

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Foundation: read the diagram. HT: formal notation for independent events (E4a) and conditional probability (E4b). Tree diagrams with replacement vs without replacement is the most error-prone subtopic — drill both.

lessons_in_batch.title: Comparing Data Sets in Context
lessons_in_batch.description: Picking the right average and spread measure for the task, comparing two distributions with full context-based interpretations.
section_markers: compare sample data to population data

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Spec note: comparisons must be context-based interpretations, not just observations of difference. Highest-marks-lost area on Paper 2. Foundation = range; HT adds IQR + standard deviation comparisons. Silver and gold problems must force context-based reasoning.

lessons_in_batch.title: Normal Distribution and Standardising Data
lessons_in_batch.description: Properties of the Normal curve, the 68/95 results within standard deviations, and standardising data to compare across samples.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Higher-only lesson. All 20 problems have higher_only: true. Spec note: no calculations for Normal probabilities beyond the 68/95 result. Standardising formula will be given. Test-score comparison context (z-style) is the canonical worked example.

lessons_in_batch.title: Quality Control Charts, Population Estimates and Capture–Recapture
lessons_in_batch.description: Action and warning lines in quality control, estimating a population mean from a sample, and the Petersen capture–recapture formula.
section_markers: validity and reliability of capture recapture

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Higher-only lesson. All 20 problems have higher_only: true. Petersen formula = (sample1 × sample2) / number marked in sample2 (given in spec formula list). The three assumptions question is a frequent 2-mark drop: (1) closed population, (2) marks do not fall off, (3) equal capture probability.
